newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada's national net worth up four pct in 1996.
newsitem.headline: Canada's national net worth up four pct in 1996.

text.p: Canada's national net worth rose almost four percent to C$2.6 trillion in 1996, while the average Canadian's worth advanced C$2,100, Statistics Canada said on Monday.
The 2.5 percent rise, to C$85,000 from C$82,900 in 1995 was the combined result of an increase in national wealth and a small decline in Canada's net foreign indebtedness, the federal agency said.
Net worth grew at a slightly faster pace than last year, reflecting the strength in domestic economic activity and the slowing in debt accumulation, Statscan said.

National wealth, the sum of non-financial assets in all sectors of the economy, rose about three percent to reach C$2.9 trillion, in line with the rise in domestic expenditures in 1996, the agency said.
National net worth is wealth less what is owed to non- residents.

The change in wealth was broadly based. The increase in residential property was in line with the pick-up in the market in the year, Statscan said. Growth in durable goods stemmed from renewed consumer spending, especially on automobiles.
The advance in machinery and equipment resulted from relatively strong business investment, while agricultural land was also up, partly due to the gain in grain prices.
The non-residential construction sector saw the weakest growth, mainly because of a drop in government investment.

The agency said that stock market activity helped corporations continue to strengthen their balance sheets. Strong share issues, along with healthy profits, led to a further decline in the debt-to-equity ratio, which has trended downward for the last six years.

Household net worth advanced strongly, with a five percent increase in debt offset by similar increases in assets. But because absolute net worth is greater than debt, this led to an increase of five percent in net worth, Statscan said. The ratio of debt to net worth remained flat in 1996, it said.
